H1 Policy Comparison: Same-Day Release of Unused Reservations

Policies optimized for average appointment utilization

Main findings

  • Most policy comparisons are still ties. Both-flexible improves on baseline in 28.7% of backgrounds and is practically tied in 70.8%.
  • Release makes reservations more useful. Reservation-only improves on baseline in 22.5%, compared with fewer backgrounds in the strict companion analysis.
  • Both-flexible is usually tied with reservation-only. Their difference is a practical tie in 92.6% of backgrounds.
  • Reservation-only more often beats horizon-only than the reverse. It wins in 111 backgrounds, loses in 61, and ties in 666.
  • Patient-group redistribution remains important. Priority served rate rises while general-group served rate falls in 37.5% of reservation-only comparisons with baseline.

How the simulations were run

  • 840 backgrounds: 42 anchor settings and 798 Sobol-sampled settings.
  • 10 paired seeds were used for every evaluated policy cell.
  • Demand-to-capacity ratio ranged from 0.8 to 3.0; priority-group share ranged from 0.1 to 0.9.
  • Daily capacity ranged from 20 to 50 slots and the native horizon ranged from 2 to 26 days.
  • Cancellation, balking, and no-show behavior varied across both groups.
  • Paired bootstrap intervals used 2,000 draws. A difference within 0.005 utilization was treated as a practical tie.

The four policy regimes were:

Policy Booking horizon Priority reservations
Baseline Fixed at the background value None
Horizon only Optimized None
Reservation only Fixed at the background value Quantity and reservation window optimized
Both flexible Optimized Quantity and reservation window optimized

The primary objective was average utilization:

Class 1 and Class 2 remain different simulated patient populations in every regime. Class 1 is called the priority group only when (Q>0). When (Q=0), both groups book through the general first-come-first-served pool.

Overall policy comparison

  • Both-flexible weakly contains the other policy choices, so it cannot be worse after optimization.
  • That does not mean both policies are always needed. Most backgrounds are practical ties.
  • Reservation-only and horizon-only should be read as competing single-policy options, not as a ranking that applies to every clinic.
Comparison Median difference Supported increase Practical tie
Both flexible − baseline 0.23 pp 28.7% 70.8%
Both flexible − horizon only 0.15 pp 15.4% 84.4%
Both flexible − reservation only 0.02 pp 7.4% 92.6%
Horizon only − baseline 0.00 pp 15.6% 84.4%
Reservation only − baseline 0.17 pp 22.5% 77.1%
Reservation only − horizon only 0.09 pp 13.2% 79.3%

Which scenarios benefit?

The dominant pattern is demand pressure:

  • At low and moderate demand, the policies are usually tied in utilization.
  • The clearest gains appear when demand approaches the upper end of the tested range.
  • Priority-group share changes which single policy performs better, but it does not create one universal winner.

No-show behavior and reservation value

With same-day release:

  • Demand remains the strongest separator between ties and meaningful utilization gains.
  • Reservations begin to show modest gains across a wider range of priority-group shares because unused reserved slots can be reused.
  • At a demand-to-capacity ratio of 3.0, the median reservation-only gain rises from about 0.3 pp to about 3.6 pp as the general-group low-delay no-show probability rises from 0.05 to 0.30.
  • The incremental value of horizon flexibility after reservations are optimized is usually small: both-flexible and reservation-only tie in most backgrounds.

Optimized policy parameters

The figure below focuses on both-flexible, where the horizon, reserved quantity, and reservation window were jointly selected.

Release changes how the nominal reservation parameters should be interpreted:

  • The jointly optimized horizon is 2 days in 44.5% of backgrounds and 6 days in 37.4%.
  • Optimized (Q) is often large—commonly 75%–90% of daily capacity across priority-group shares.
  • A large (Q) does not mean that the same share is withheld from the general group for the full day. Unused reservations are released.
  • Release therefore makes high nominal reservation caps less costly than under the strict policy.
  • Reservation windows are generally longer than under strict reservation when the horizon is fixed, but remain short under many jointly optimized settings.

Effects on the two patient groups

The utilization objective counts completed appointments, regardless of which group receives them. A utilization gain can therefore coexist with a redistribution of access.

  • Horizon changes can help or hurt either group because they change the set of delays offered to everyone.
  • Reservations more directly redistribute access toward Class 1.
  • “Priority gains; general loses” means the paired confidence intervals support both directions. It is not inferred from point estimates alone.

The main strict-reservation trade-off appears under congested conditions:

  • Reservation-only produces a supported priority-gain/general-loss pattern in 37.5% of backgrounds.
  • Both-flexible produces the same pattern in 38.2%.
  • At demand ratios below 1.2, clear group changes are rare.
  • As demand rises, reservations increasingly determine who receives limited capacity rather than creating additional capacity.

Comparison with the twice-weighted Class 1 objective

The secondary objective was:

[ = . ]

Class 1 therefore receives twice the policy weight of Class 2.

What is similar?

  • The baseline is identical because it has no parameters to optimize.
  • Demand remains the main condition under which policy changes matter.
  • Short horizons remain common under both objectives.
  • Horizon-only is more stable across objectives than reservation policies.

What changes?

Policy Same exact policy cell Median average-utilization change Median weighted-rate change Average-utilization loss > 0.5 pp Weighted-rate gain > 0.5 pp Priority gains; general loses
Both flexible 11.5% -0.20 pp 0.36 pp 23.5% 44.0% 26.7%
Horizon only 71.0% 0.00 pp 0.00 pp 3.8% 13.0% 8.5%
Reservation only 21.1% -0.14 pp 0.19 pp 21.2% 35.8% 22.0%

The weighted objective still changes reservation design, but release softens the capacity cost:

  • For reservation-only, switching to the weighted optimum changes average utilization by a median of -0.14 pp and raises the weighted served rate by 0.19 pp.
  • For both-flexible, the corresponding medians are -0.20 pp and 0.36 pp.
  • Exact reservation cells remain uncommon across objectives, but the median utilization loss is smaller than under strict reservation.
  • The largest differences are in (Q), reservation-window length, and Class 1 versus Class 2 access—not in the overall demand pattern.

Brief comparison with the companion report

The strict-reservation report has the same central result: meaningful utilization gains concentrate under heavy demand.

Compared with strict reservation:

  • Release increases the share of backgrounds where reservation-only improves utilization.
  • Release supports much larger nominal (Q) values because unused reservations can return to the general pool.
  • The twice-weighted Class 1 objective causes a smaller average-utilization loss under release.
  • Strict reservation requires more conservative reserved quantities and shorter reservation windows to avoid stranded capacity.

Conclusions

  • Low and moderate demand: practical ties remain the dominant result.
  • Heavy demand: horizon flexibility and reservations can both improve utilization; the largest gains occur when no-show risk is also high.
  • Release effect: reservation-only performs better relative to horizon-only than under strict reservation, while both-flexible is usually tied with reservation-only.
  • Access distribution: release protects capacity use but does not eliminate priority-group gains at the general group’s expense.
  • Objective choice matters: the twice-weighted Class 1 objective changes reservation design, although release reduces its utilization cost.
